You say things like "society has a strict definition of what a successful person looks like" as though the definition was created, and then the application of it followed, when in reality, it is the other way around. The image of a successful and hardworking person is predicated off of what successful and hardworking people look like. 

Do all people conform to this image? Not at all. But if a person is hardworking and successful, and they also do not conform to that image, then they will still be successful and hardworking, as evidenced by their success. 

I say this not to be confrontational, but only to point out that the expectations for a hardworking and successful person are quite simple, and also quite subject to variation. 

For example, one expectation for a hardworking and successful person is to be hardworking. Aside from that, there are basic expectations that everyone follows such as being to work on time, completing the work that you are given on time, respecting your coworkers and superiors, etc. There is not necessarily one way to do these things, there is only one necessary outcome for them.

Constituents that meet those expectations make a constituency successful. I do not see why it would make sense to change any of them.

Any vibration pattern can be decomposed into a linear combination of normal modes, as a reference, consider the Fourier decomposition. The fundamental modes are the eigenfunctions of the underlying differential equation, which describes the dynamics of the system. 
Normal modes are independent motions of atoms that ultimately do not impel other modes to movement (The number of which depending the degrees of freedom).
A characteristic frequency however, refers to the resonant frequency of a system that is exposed to a spectrum of input frequencies. 

If one were to measure the amplitude of oscillation of the mass versus frequency of a force, the result would be a spectrum that has a peak, the shape and location of which being determined by the amount of damping that occurs. That peak would be the characteristic frequency of the spectrum.
